methodology: Gospels and Acts are primary evidence for the episodes; OT references illuminate the broader history of a named region, not evidence Jesus visited that Old Testament event. Independent archaeological scholarship is cited where available. Absence of an external archaeology citation is explicitly not proof of a site identification.

bethlehem.historicalContext: Judean settlement associated with David and his family; the Gospels place Jesus' birth here.
bethlehem.archaeology: The Church of the Nativity marks a site venerated from at least the second century; the church was first completed in the fourth century. This preserves early tradition, not an excavated first-century birth certificate.

oldTestament.note: Bethlehem in the prophetic royal context

bethlehem.caution: The Gospel names the town; the precise building or cave is identified by later Christian tradition.

jerusalem.historicalContext: Temple and pilgrimage centre in the first century. Jesus is shown attending feasts, teaching, and facing trial and crucifixion there.
jerusalem.archaeology: Regev and colleagues report 103 radiocarbon measurements across five excavation areas, supporting an Iron Age urban chronology and identifying regional calibration offsets. Radiocarbon dates organic samples in archaeological contexts. Calibration, stratigraphy and modelling affect interpretation; the study does not date every building or independently establish every biblical event.
jerusalem.caution: A city-level identification does not establish the location of the upper room, trial, Golgotha or tomb.

egypt.historicalContext: Egypt is named as a refuge for the family in Matthew 2, echoing Israel's earlier history in Egypt.
egypt.archaeology: The Gospel records no Egyptian town, route, dates or particular residence. Archaeological sites elsewhere in Egypt cannot identify the family's lodging.

oldTestament.note: Matthew applies the wording to Jesus in Matthew 2:15

egypt.caution: The map pin is a regional placeholder, not an archaeological claim or a travel destination.

nazareth.historicalContext: Jesus' upbringing and synagogue appearance are connected to a rural Galilean community.
nazareth.archaeology: Excavations document settlement in the Late Hellenistic and Early Roman periods and a Jewish farming community. None of the excavated homes is securely identifiable as the specific childhood house of Jesus.
nazareth.caution: Nazareth is not specifically named in the Old Testament; proposed connections are later interpretations.

jordan.modernSetting: Jordan River valley - baptism reach uncertain
jordan.historicalContext: Jesus is baptised in the Jordan by John; the river connects the narrative to Israel's crossing traditions.
jordan.archaeology: Al-Maghtas on the eastern bank has Roman and Byzantine pilgrim remains and is recognised as a traditional baptism site. Such remains evidence later devotion, not a pinpoint first-century baptism location.
jordan.caution: The location of the baptism cannot be independently fixed to a precise riverbank coordinate.

wilderness.historicalContext: The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus' temptation in the wilderness without naming the site.
wilderness.archaeology: A wide desert and upland landscape is relevant; a named cave or mountain cannot be verified from the passages alone.

oldTestament.note: Wilderness-testing motif invoked in the temptation account

wilderness.caution: The pin represents a broad region. Do not treat the traditional Mount of Temptation as a proven site.

beyond-jordan.modernSetting: East bank of the Jordan - several proposed sites
beyond-jordan.historicalContext: John places the Baptist's ministry and a later retreat beyond the Jordan.
beyond-jordan.archaeology: Al-Maghtas preserves evidence of ancient Christian pilgrimage and baptisms; the first-century locality and its relationship to all Bethany references remain debated.

oldTestament.note: Earlier crossing narrative in the Jordan corridor

beyond-jordan.caution: Do not confuse Bethany beyond the Jordan with Bethany near Jerusalem.

cana.modernSetting: Lower Galilee - candidate sites near modern Kafr Kanna and Khirbet Qana
cana.historicalContext: John records the wedding sign and healing linked to Cana.
cana.archaeology: Multiple archaeological and traditional proposals remain in use. The precise site is disputed, so no candidate is asserted as definite.
cana.caution: The biblical name is clear but the exact modern identification is not established.

capernaum.modernSetting: Tell Hum, northwest Sea of Galilee
capernaum.historicalContext: A major setting for Jesus' Galilean teaching, healings and residence, with repeated visits in the Gospels.
capernaum.archaeology: Archaeological remains include Roman-period basalt homes, a synagogue complex and later Christian memorial structures. The conspicuous limestone synagogue is later than Jesus' ministry, though earlier levels exist.

oldTestament.note: Regional Galilee context cited by Matthew 4:13-16, not the town name

capernaum.caution: Later commemorative buildings cannot by themselves confirm a particular miracle or house owner.

judea-region.modernSetting: Judean hills and valleys - unnamed setting
judea-region.historicalContext: John describes Jesus and his disciples ministering in Judea without identifying a town.
judea-region.archaeology: Archaeological remains occur throughout Judea, but none can identify this unspecified stage of John's account.
judea-region.caution: No city should be inferred from John 3:22.

sychar.modernSetting: Vicinity of modern Nablus, West Bank
sychar.historicalContext: John situates Jesus' meeting with a Samaritan woman by Jacob's well.
sychar.archaeology: Abu Alsaud and colleagues dated human remains recovered beside the commemorated well and monastery, supporting later burial and pilgrimage chronology. Dates of human remains do not date the cutting of the well, identify its biblical user or establish Sychar's town limits. Proposed links to named people or historical events remain interpretations.
sychar.caution: Shechem is not automatically identical to the town called Sychar.

identificationReview.question: Does the identification of Jacob's Well establish the location of Sychar?
identificationReview.claim: John 4 identifies Sychar near land associated with Jacob, while the modern well and surrounding settlement history have distinct evidence. Sychar, ancient Shechem and later Nablus should not be casually equated.
identificationReview.support: Radiocarbon work at Jacob's Well concerns dated human remains and later site history. Pummer analyses historical usage of Shechem and Samaritan history, providing regional context without identifying the Gospel town.
identificationReview.limit: Dating material from the well complex neither proves the identity of the woman nor fixes the first-century settlement boundaries of Sychar.

ancientNames: Kinneret / Lake Gennesaret / Sea of Tiberias
galilee-shore.modernSetting: Sea of Galilee - exact shore landing varies
galilee-shore.historicalContext: Boats, fishing communities, teaching and miracles are repeatedly associated with the lake. The Jairus episode is conservatively mapped to the lakeshore as Mark 5:21 does not name Capernaum.
galilee-shore.archaeology: The lake and its regional settlement network are geographically secure; specific boat courses and shoreline landing sites are usually not supplied.

oldTestament.note: Chinnereth among fortified towns; name linked to the lake region

galilee-shore.caution: The point is only a navigational marker for lake episodes, not the location of each miracle.

galilee-hill.historicalContext: Matthew describes mountain teaching; Luke describes related teaching on a level place.
galilee-hill.archaeology: No excavated place identifies the exact Sermon on the Mount hillside. The well-known traditional landscape is later pilgrimage geography.
galilee-hill.caution: Do not identify the traditional pilgrimage site as a biblically named hill.

nain.historicalContext: Luke locates the restoration of a widow's son at the gate of Nain.
nain.archaeology: The modern village is usually associated with Nain. Excavation does not establish the Gospel meeting point or city gate.
nain.caution: Ancient town limits and the particular gate remain uncertain.

east-shore.modernSetting: Eastern shore of Galilee - competing districts
east-shore.historicalContext: Gospel accounts use different geographical designations for the deliverance of a possessed man or men.
east-shore.archaeology: The Kursi Beach report documents a breakwater and public-building remains with Byzantine, Umayyad and early Abbasid evidence. Kursi Beach is distinct from the nearby monastery. Later settlement remains do not establish a first-century landing point or resolve Gerasenes/Gadarenes/Gergesenes readings.
east-shore.caution: Place variants in manuscript traditions and Gospel accounts should not be hidden.

bethsaida.modernSetting: Northeastern Sea of Galilee - el-Araj and et-Tell candidates
bethsaida.historicalContext: Fishing-community associations and several signs/healings are located at or near Bethsaida.
bethsaida.archaeology: Excavations at el-Araj have documented Roman and Byzantine materials; et-Tell is another proposed identification. The archaeological identification remains contested.
bethsaida.caution: Both el-Araj and et-Tell appear in identification debates. The el-Araj season report confirms excavated material, not a consensus that it is the Gospel Bethsaida.

identificationReview.question: Which archaeological site corresponds to the Bethsaida of the Gospel accounts?
identificationReview.claim: El-Araj and et-Tell are competing proposed identifications. The available reports support archaeological occupation and rival geographic arguments, not a scholarly consensus or the exact locations of individual Gospel episodes.
identificationReview.support: The el-Araj excavation team reports Roman-period occupation and material near the lakeshore; Arav publishes a competing scholarly case for et-Tell. Both contributions are researcher positions and must be read with provenance.
identificationReview.limit: Neither excavation directly identifies a site of the feeding, healing or a specific disciple's house. The unverified alternative must remain visible.

gennesaret.historicalContext: A fertile plain receiving Jesus and the disciples after a crossing, with people bringing the sick.
gennesaret.archaeology: The plain is geographically recognisable. The text does not locate a single verified disembarkation or house.
gennesaret.caution: Gennesaret can mean a shore region; a point marker is approximate.

sidon.historicalContext: Mark describes a route through Sidon and surrounding territory on the way towards the Decapolis.
sidon.archaeology: Sidon is a long-lived coastal city with archaeological layers. The text does not specify which buildings or streets Jesus used.

oldTestament.note: Prophetic reference to the Phoenician coast

sidon.caution: A region or transit corridor must not be converted into a list of unrecorded city meetings.

decapolis.modernSetting: East and southeast of the Sea of Galilee
decapolis.historicalContext: The Gospels speak of Decapolis as a region, not a single point or one fixed itinerary.
decapolis.archaeology: Roman-period city ruins are documented across the territory, but the event is not assigned to a particular Decapolis city.
decapolis.caution: The marker is a representative regional point; city-level visit claims would be ungrounded.

ancientNames: Dalmanutha in Mark; Magdala suggested but not certain
magadan.modernSetting: Western shore, Sea of Galilee - precise site disputed
magadan.historicalContext: Matthew and Mark use different location names for the landing after the feeding.
magadan.archaeology: The ancient town of Magdala/Migdal has excavated Early Roman remains, but these do not prove Magadan and Dalmanutha are the same location.
magadan.caution: Distinguish well-attested Magdala archaeology from uncertain Magadan/Dalmanutha identification.

identificationReview.question: Are Magadan, Dalmanutha and later Magdala the same location?
identificationReview.claim: Matthew 15:39 and Mark 8:10 name Magadan and Dalmanutha respectively; later Magdala traditions and excavated sites require a separate identification argument. Equating the names remains a proposal.
identificationReview.support: Excavations at the modern Magdala site establish an ancient settlement. Joan E. Taylor proposes a relationship among Magadan, Dalmanutha and later Magdala naming, explicitly as a research interpretation.
identificationReview.limit: Ancient settlement evidence at Magdala does not confirm that Jesus' boat landed at that precise excavation or that Dalmanutha is its securely attested synonym.

caesarea-philippi.historicalContext: The district provides the backdrop for Peter's confession and following teaching in the Gospels.
caesarea-philippi.archaeology: Ancient Paneas/Banias is historically attested, including Roman-era religious remains; the conversations could have occurred elsewhere in the district.
caesarea-philippi.caution: The Gospels name the district or villages of Caesarea Philippi, not a proven conversation site inside the town or at a modern shrine.

mountain.modernSetting: High mountain - not specified in the Gospels
mountain.historicalContext: Matthew, Mark and Luke describe the Transfiguration without naming the mountain.
mountain.archaeology: The Tabor trial excavation documents medieval fortification; Puig i Tarrech's note 34 discusses Tabor, Hermon and Golan proposals while leaving the mountain unknown. Medieval remains do not identify a first-century event. The scholarly note supports preserving an unnamed mountain, not endorsing Tabor or Hermon; the full article remains unread.
mountain.caution: The schematic map pin represents a mountain setting, not a located peak.

samaria-region.historicalContext: Luke records an unnamed Samaritan village refusing hospitality.
samaria-region.archaeology: Excavations throughout Samaria cannot identify this unnamed village from the source.
samaria-region.caution: No modern village identification is claimed.

border.modernSetting: Between Samaria and Galilee - unspecified route
border.historicalContext: Luke describes travel between regions during the healing of ten men with leprosy.
border.archaeology: No individual town or road segment is identified; boundaries varied over time.
border.caution: The exact border location is not recorded.

jordan-east.historicalContext: Matthew and Mark discuss ministry across the Jordan without a detailed list of stops.
jordan-east.archaeology: The broader corridor is identifiable but there is no specific excavated site attached to this journey step.
jordan-east.caution: Perea is a geographic frame, not a biblical claim about this marker.

bethany.historicalContext: John places Lazarus, Mary and Martha in Bethany, a repeated stop near Jerusalem.
bethany.archaeology: The excavation monograph catalogue covers village remains and successive churches. The site project traces tomb commemoration to late antiquity and describes later alterations. The full monograph remains unread. The project account supports the history of veneration, not an independently demonstrated identification of Lazarus's burial or a miracle.
bethany.caution: This is separate from Bethany beyond the Jordan.

ephraim.historicalContext: John reports a withdrawal to Ephraim near the wilderness.
ephraim.archaeology: Murphy-O'Connor favours Taiybeh for John's Ephraim. Keinan and colleagues argue for Khirbet Marjameh in early Hebrew geography. The studies address different textual and historical scopes; their Ephraim references cannot automatically be equated. Abstract-only access does not settle John's town or justify moving its marker.
ephraim.caution: The marker should not be treated as a surveyed first-century city centre.

ancientNames: Tell es-Sultan (ancient mound); Roman/Herodian Jericho (different occupation zones)
jericho.historicalContext: Jericho features in Old Testament conquest tradition and Jesus' final journey, including the healing and Zacchaeus.
jericho.archaeology: Bruins and van der Plicht analysed 18 samples, distinguishing short-lived cereal grains from charcoal. Their published calibration placed the final Middle Bronze Age destruction in the late seventeenth or sixteenth century BCE. This is the study's reported 1995 calibration, not a new calculation. It must not be relabelled as a secure fifteenth- or thirteenth-century conquest date; archaeological destruction alone identifies neither attackers nor a biblical event.
jericho.caution: The UNESCO-listed Tell es-Sultan contains prehistoric and Bronze Age remains; it is not itself evidence for the exact New Testament-era town setting or healing site.

bethphage.modernSetting: Eastern approach to Jerusalem - near the Mount of Olives
bethphage.historicalContext: The Gospels name Bethphage as a village near the Jerusalem approach and Mount of Olives, then describe disciples sent to obtain a donkey from a village ahead.
bethphage.archaeology: Mizrachi reports rock-cut installations and caves on Bethphage's eastern slopes, including Byzantine material and a tentatively dated Second Temple burial cave. Some caves were unexcavated or incompletely documented. Nearby remains do not establish the Gospel village boundary, the donkey retrieval village or a particular street.
bethphage.caution: The Gospels do not state that the donkey was fetched specifically inside Bethphage; its ancient village footprint also remains uncertain.

olives.historicalContext: Connected with Jesus' approach, final discourse, prayer vicinity and ascension narrative.
olives.archaeology: The IAA report documents a damaged burial cave about 500 m north of the Church of Gethsemane. Pottery and ossuary lids support first-century CE use. This is a typological and contextual archaeological date, not a radiocarbon measurement. A burial cave does not locate a discourse, prayer or ascension.

oldTestament.note: David ascends the Mount of Olives
Prophetic reference to the Mount of Olives

olives.caution: The Mount of Olives spans a ridge, not a single pinpoint coordinate.

gethsemane.modernSetting: Foot of the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem
gethsemane.historicalContext: The Synoptic Gospels recount prayer and arrest in a place called Gethsemane.
gethsemane.archaeology: Bernabei reports successful dating of three of eight olive trees to the twelfth century; the other five were not dated. An IAA announcement describes a Second Temple-period ritual bath and later church remains nearby. Hollow trunks limit sampling; these results neither date all trees nor establish first-century roots. The bath supports period activity, not the exact prayer location; proposed oil production remains tentative.
gethsemane.caution: The traditional gardens are later commemorations of an event tied by Scripture to an area, not a measured plot.

identificationReview.question: Can later garden tradition or excavated features locate the exact site of Jesus' prayer?
identificationReview.claim: The Synoptic accounts name Gethsemane and the Mount of Olives area, while a modern pilgrimage garden is not an independently surveyed Gospel event location.
identificationReview.support: Published tree-age research addresses sampled living olives; an excavation announcement reports Second Temple-era remains in the vicinity. Both are evidence of vegetation or occupation, not the precise prayer location.
identificationReview.limit: Dating the cores of surviving trees or nearby features does not identify the precise garden boundary in the first century or authenticate any single prayer spot.

emmaus.modernSetting: West of Jerusalem - candidate sites vary
emmaus.historicalContext: Luke records a road encounter and meal following the resurrection.
emmaus.archaeology: The Moza report proposes identifying its Middle Roman settlement with the Emmaus/Colonia of Vespasian's veterans. That proposed post-revolt identification does not establish Luke's Emmaus. Nicopolis, el-Qubeibeh and other proposals, the distance variants and their chronology still need comparative assessment.
emmaus.caution: The map point is illustrative and does not select one candidate as definitive.

identificationReview.question: Which Emmaus village is intended by Luke 24:13?
identificationReview.claim: Luke names Emmaus but the modern identification remains unresolved. The approximately sixty-stadia reading is commonly printed; other manuscript traditions report a longer distance, adding complexity to proposed sites.
identificationReview.support: A published archaeological report documents Roman-era material near Moza, and Robinson's scholarly article discusses Emmaus as a narrative destination of uncertain location.
identificationReview.limit: Moza, Emmaus-Nicopolis and other proposed sites cannot be selected as conclusively verified from this dossier. Textual-variant questions require their own manuscript collation.

galilee-mountain.historicalContext: Matthew places the commissioning of disciples on a mountain in Galilee without identifying it.
galilee-mountain.archaeology: A specific excavated mountain site cannot be matched to the passage.
galilee-mountain.caution: Do not conflate this unnamed location with the Transfiguration mountain.

tyre.historicalContext: A prominent Phoenician port in the Old Testament; Jesus visits its district in the Gospel narratives.
tyre.archaeology: UNESCO documents Phoenician and substantial Roman-period remains at Tyre; excavation establishes the ancient city, not a particular Gospel house.

oldTestament.note: Relations between Solomon and Hiram of Tyre

tyre.caution: Mark 7 places Jesus in the territory of Tyre; it does not identify an excavated dwelling.

galilee-region.historicalContext: The northern region is prominent in prophetic wording and in the Gospels as the setting of Jesus' early ministry.
galilee-region.archaeology: Archaeological sites document varied Galilean settlements. No single archaeological site identifies this region-wide travel entry.

Kedesh in Galilee named as a refuge city

galilee-region.caution: A regional episode must not be presented as an individually evidenced town visit.

audit.scope: Location/source metadata checked for 35 place dossiers. Text of external literature not independently peer reviewed by this project. Source links checked 26 October 2026.
audit.verification: Bibliographic and location-confidence screening; scholarly review remains ongoing.

identificationAddendum.method: Five contested/traditional locations received claim-to-source assessments of competing interpretations. All 35 place records were checked for explicit evidence levels, original sources and consistent study notes. Twelve deliberately regional or unnamed locations retain no independent place-site bibliography instead of receiving misleading exact-site sources.
identificationAddendum.limits: This is a bounded AI-assisted review of publication metadata, accessible academic abstracts, project reports and existing sources. Specialist archaeological review, manuscript collation and exhaustive original excavation-text checking remain open.
